title: Design like Karpathy is watching — Zeke Sikelianos, Replicate

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is about making developer platforms and tools LLM-native, with Replicate's API, documentation, Cog, and MCP server as the substrate other engineers build on. The domain is developer_platforms because the talk centers on tools and platforms used by software builders including Replicate, Cog, MCP servers, and API documentation systems. The talk covers design through build, deploy, and documentation stages, as illustrated by Karpathy's MenuGen journey from local development to production deployment pain. The talk requires familiarity with APIs, LLMs, and developer tooling but does not demand deep ML expertise. This is a recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair. Multiple direct transcript quotes with character positions ground the classification in specific spoken content from the talk.

summary: Zeke Sikelianos, a developer tools veteran at Replicate, introduces Andrej Karpathy as an AI researcher (Google, OpenAI, Tesla, Eureka Labs), YouTube educator, coiner of vibe coding, and author of the Software 2.0 manifesto. The talk centers on MenuGen, an app Karpathy built at a hackathon that generates image representations of restaurant menu items from text-menu photos. Karpathy blogged about the experience, calling local development an exhilarating escapade but deployment a painful slog, and raked multiple companies including Replicate over the coals for poor developer experience. Specifically for Replicate, the LLM's knowledge was outdated, docs were out of date, the API had changed, and rate limiting created friction. Replicate blocked Karpathy's account via an abuse-detection false positive, but their CEO saw the blog post and unblocked him—something not every user can leverage. Zeke frames this as embarrassing but an opportunity to improve. Replicate's responses include embracing llm.txt for markdown-based documentation LLMs can consume more easily than HTML, adding copy-as-markdown and send-to-Claude/ChatGPT buttons on model pages, leveraging curl commands as LLM-native API references, packaging models with Cog (whose docs are now a single llm.txt file), and building an MCP server from their existing OpenAPI schema installable in Claude Desktop with one JSON config line. Zeke then distills actionable lessons: accept upfront credit payments so power users can pay and avoid false-positive bans, document everything when shipping features (it's not done until it's documented and LLMs can consume it), feed the machines by producing content in LLM-friendly forms, use boring well-established technologies like SQL that LLMs already know well, and practice good API hygiene by keeping JSON responses slim and information-dense for LLM context windows. In Q&A, he recommends starting doc generation with OpenAPI schemas in YAML or JSON, using tools like Docusaurus, Read the Docs, or Readme.com to generate docs and SDKs. He also addresses LLM-driven purchasing decisions, arguing that APIs should expose structured data like pricing so LLMs can compare models on cost, speed, and quality without requiring humans to visit web pages. The overarching thesis is that the primary audience for developer products, services, and libraries is now LLMs, not humans.

sections.title: Introduction and audience interaction
sections.summary: Zeke opens with audience participation gauging familiarity with Karpathy and identifying Replicate employees in the room.

sections.title: Who is Andrej Karpathy
sections.summary: Zeke introduces Karpathy as an AI researcher at Google, OpenAI, Tesla, and Eureka Labs, a YouTube educator, coiner of vibe coding, and author of the Software 2.0 manifesto predicting ML models would write code.

sections.title: MenuGen and the deployment pain
sections.summary: MenuGen is a web app that generates food images from text-menu photos. Karpathy built it at a hackathon, describing local development as exhilarating but deployment as a painful slog. His blog post criticized developer experience across multiple companies including Replicate, whose outdated docs, outdated LLM knowledge, API changes, and rate limiting created friction.

sections.title: llm.txt and documentation improvements
sections.summary: Replicate embraced llm.txt, serving markdown-based documentation optimized for LLM consumption. They added features on model pages to copy content as markdown, send it to Claude, or send it to ChatGPT, enabling interactive exploration of model capabilities rather than passive web reading.

sections.title: curl and Cog for LLM-friendly tooling
sections.summary: Zeke cites Karpathy's observation that LLMs don't like to click, they like to curl, arguing curl commands encode everything needed for API requests. Replicate's Cog tool packages ML models in Docker containers with standardized OpenAPI interfaces, and its docs are available as a single llm.txt file for editor consumption.

sections.title: MCP and OpenAPI integration
sections.summary: Zeke explains MCP as a way to make OpenAPI schemas actionable for language models. Replicate built an MCP server from their existing OpenAPI schema, installable in Claude Desktop with one JSON config line, enabling discovery, search, and project scaffolding without separate software installation.

sections.title: Note to self: remaining issues and abuse detection
sections.summary: Zeke acknowledges remaining issues including abuse-detection false positives that flagged Karpathy's legitimate high-volume API usage shortly after account creation, triggering rate limiting despite being a paid user.

sections.title: Lessons: payments, documentation, boring tech, API hygiene
sections.summary: Zeke distills actionable lessons from the Karpathy incident: accept upfront credit payments so power users can self-serve without triggering abuse detection, document everything when shipping features (it's not done until LLMs can consume it), feed the machines by producing LLM-friendly content, use boring well-established technologies like SQL that LLMs know well, and practice good API hygiene by keeping JSON responses slim and information-dense for LLM context windows.

sections.title: Q&A: doc generation and LLM-driven purchasing decisions
sections.summary: In Q&A, Zeke recommends starting doc generation with OpenAPI schemas in YAML or JSON, using tools like Docusaurus, Read the Docs, and Readme.com. He also addresses LLM-driven purchasing decisions, arguing APIs should expose structured data like pricing so LLMs can compare models on cost, speed, and quality without humans visiting web pages.
